opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. You know, grasping is one of those things that seems trivially easy because we do it all the time without thinking. A two-year-old can pick up a toy they've never seen before. But for robots, it's remarkably hard, and I think it's worth unpacking why.

The core issue is uncertainty, and it shows up in three places. First, there's uncertainty in perception. A robot's cameras and depth sensors are noisy. They struggle with shiny surfaces, transparent objects, and things that are partially hidden behind other things. So the robot never has a perfect picture of the object's shape or exactly where it sits.

Second, there's uncertainty in control. Even if you know exactly where you want the gripper to go, the motors, gears, and joints have small errors. A few millimeters off can be the difference between a secure grasp and the object slipping or getting knocked over.

And third, there's uncertainty in physics. That's the part people often underestimate. We don't know the friction coefficient of the surface, the exact mass distribution of the object, or how it'll deform. Contact mechanics is notoriously difficult to model. Small changes in where your fingers touch can produce very different outcomes.

What makes it especially tricky is that these uncertainties compound. So a lot of our work, for instance with Dex-Net, has been about embracing that uncertainty rather than trying to eliminate it. Instead of searching for the theoretically perfect grasp, we look for grasps that are *robust*, ones that will succeed even if the object is a little different from what we think, or the gripper lands slightly off target. We combined analytic models of grasp mechanics with large amounts of synthetic data and deep learning, and that turned out to be quite powerful.

But I always want to be careful not to overstate progress. There's a lot of excitement right now, and robots have gotten much better at picking objects out of bins in warehouses, for example. But in unstructured environments like a home, with clutter and endless variety, reliable grasping is still an open problem. I sometimes call this the gap between what people think robots can do and what they actually can do, and I think it's important to be honest about it.

r001.rationale: The response says motors, gears, and joints have small errors, so the gripper can miss its intended position by a few millimeters.

r002.rationale: Deep learning is mentioned as part of Dex-Net, but the response does not say it compensates for motor positioning errors.

r003.rationale: The response describes noisy cameras and depth sensors, but does not state that stereo vision fails to provide an accurate spatial map of the surroundings.

r004.rationale: The response contrasts effortless human grasping with robotic difficulty, but does not attribute human spatial perception to prior understanding of how the world works.

r005.rationale: The response says a few millimeters of error can cause a poor or slipping grasp, but does not say an object-position perception error can make the robot collide with the object.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a great question, and it gets at something I've been thinking about for over 30 years. People are often surprised when I tell them that grasping, which a two-year-old does effortlessly, is still one of the hardest problems in robotics. And the reason comes down to uncertainty.

Let me break it into the two pieces you mentioned. On the perception side, the robot has to figure out what's in front of it: where the object is, what shape it is, what the surface is like. Our sensors are nowhere near as good as human eyes. A depth camera gives you a noisy point cloud. Objects are occluded by other objects. Transparent and shiny things are notoriously hard, because the light bounces around and the sensor just doesn't return good data. So right from the start, the robot has an imperfect estimate of the world.

Then on the control side, even if you knew exactly where the object was, there's the question of exactly where your gripper ends up. Robot arms have some error. There's backlash in the gears, calibration drift between the camera and the arm. A few millimeters might not sound like much, but when you're trying to pinch a pencil or pick up a wine glass, a few millimeters is the difference between success and knocking it over.

And then there's the physics, which I think is the deepest part. When two surfaces come into contact, what happens depends on friction, and friction is one of the most poorly understood phenomena in all of physics. It depends on microscopic surface properties, on dust, on humidity. The object's center of mass might not be where you expect, because it's a box with something heavy on one side. So even a perfect perception system and a perfect arm would still face this fundamental unpredictability at the moment of contact.

What we've learned over the years is that you can't eliminate that uncertainty. You have to embrace it. So in our work, with Dex-Net for example, instead of asking "what is the single best grasp for this object," we ask "which grasps are robust?" Meaning, if my estimate of the object pose is off by a bit, if the friction is lower than I think, does this grasp still work? And it turns out some grasps are much more forgiving than others. Grasping a mug by the body is more robust than grasping it by the handle, even though the handle is what humans tend to go for.

The other thing we learned is that you can generate huge amounts of training data in simulation by sampling over all those uncertainties, millions of grasps on thousands of objects, and then train a network to predict robustness. And remarkably, that transfers to the real world pretty well, because you've trained the system to expect that the world won't match the model exactly.

So that's how I think about it. It's not one hard problem, it's several layers of uncertainty stacked on top of each other, and the way forward isn't perfect sensing or perfect control. It's designing systems that succeed even when things are a little bit wrong, which they always are.

r002.rationale: It says a network predicts grasp robustness, but does not say deep learning compensates for robot motor positioning errors.

r003.rationale: It describes noisy depth-camera data and imperfect world estimates, but does not state that stereo vision fails to ensure an accurate spatial map.

r004.rationale: It mentions that humans grasp effortlessly, but does not connect human spatial perception to prior understanding of how the world works.

r005.rationale: It says millimeter-scale arm error can lead to knocking an object over, but does not say that an error in the object's perceived position causes the robot to collide with it.

astra-6.text:
Grasping is something we do so effortlessly that it’s easy to underestimate how difficult it is. You look at a coffee cup, reach out, and pick it up. But you’re solving two closely connected problems: figuring out what’s there, and deciding how to make contact with it.

On the perception side, a robot gets an incomplete picture. A camera sees surfaces, but it can’t see the back of the object or what’s underneath it. There’s noise in the depth measurements. Shiny or transparent objects can be particularly difficult. And even if you know the shape, you may not know the mass, the friction, or whether the object will deform when you touch it.

On the control side, those uncertainties matter enormously. You can plan a beautiful motion, but if your estimate of the object’s position is slightly wrong, one finger may touch first and push it away. Apply too little force and it slips; too much and you might damage it. Contact changes the situation, so you need to respond to what actually happens, not just execute a predetermined trajectory.

The key is to connect perception and action through feedback, and to reason explicitly about uncertainty. Instead of asking, ‘What’s the best grasp if my model is exactly right?’ you ask, ‘What grasp is likely to succeed across the range of things that could actually be there?’ That shift is very important for reliability. And then you still need to detect failures and recover, because a successful demonstration is a long way from a system that works thousands of times without someone stepping in.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention deep learning or its role in compensating for motor positioning errors.

r003.rationale: It describes incomplete camera views and noisy depth measurements, but does not state that stereo vision fails to ensure an accurate spatial map.

r004.rationale: The response does not connect human spatial perception to prior understanding of how the world works.

r005.rationale: It says that if the object's estimated position is slightly wrong, a finger may touch first and push it away, clearly linking a small position error to unintended contact during a grasp.

sol-6.1.text:
I think grasping is a wonderful example of something that looks simple because we do it all the time, but actually brings together several very hard problems. You look at a cup, reach out, and pick it up without consciously calculating where your fingers should go or how much force to apply.

For a robot, first there’s uncertainty about what it’s seeing. A camera gives you an image, or perhaps a depth image, but that doesn’t tell you everything about the object’s shape, its mass, its friction, or what’s hidden behind it. And those are precisely the things that can determine whether a grasp succeeds.

Then there’s the control problem. You have to move the fingers into position, establish contact, and apply enough force to hold the object without damaging it. Contact changes the situation: the object may shift, or start to slip. So you need feedback, and you need to respond to information that is itself noisy and incomplete.

The important connection is that perception and control aren’t really separate. An action can help you perceive: you might nudge an object to get a better view or discover whether it moves freely. And what you perceive should change your action. The challenge is to make that whole loop reliable across a wide variety of objects, including ones the robot hasn’t encountered before.
